scenes.text: So, why are cardiovascular deaths falling while so many still live with it? Over fifty years, deaths from heart disease in Australia have fallen a long way. Cancer deaths have fallen much less, and the number of people diagnosed with cancer each year has gone up. Then decide: is more people diagnosed with cancer good news, bad news, or impossible to tell?

Cardiovascular disease means conditions of the heart and blood vessels, like coronary heart disease and stroke. Most of it starts with plaque narrowing the arteries. Its four measures don't move together. Mortality has fallen hugely over decades, though the fall has slowed. Incidence is falling too, mostly from less smoking and better blood pressure control. But prevalence stays high, because people now survive heart attacks and strokes that once killed them. And morbidity has shifted to years of heart failure, or disability after a stroke. Think of a bathtub: new cases pour in, the water is everyone living with it, and deaths drain out. Treatment narrows the drain, so the water stays high. So deaths fall for both reasons: fewer heart attacks happen, and more people survive them.

Cancer reads differently. Cancer is many diseases, in which abnormal cells divide without control and can invade other tissue. Mortality is falling, but more slowly. Incidence is rising as a count, mainly because the population is bigger and older, and partly because screening finds cancers once missed. Prevalence is rising strongly, because more are diagnosed and more survive. So more people diagnosed could mean more disease, the same disease found earlier, or more people living long enough to get it. And check for counts against an age-standardised rate, which adjusts for an older population. Counts can rise while that rate falls.

One measure is never enough. Picture one disease pathway: exposure to risk, onset, diagnosis, then the outcome. Prevention acts at exposure and onset. Screening acts at diagnosis. Treatment acts at the outcome. Incidence reads onset, so it falls only if prevention works. Mortality reads the outcome, and it falls if prevention or treatment improves, so on its own, it can't tell you which one worked.

Now the risk factors, sorted two ways. Non-modifiable factors can't be changed: age, sex, family history and inherited genes. Age is the biggest of all, so an ageing population adds cases even if nothing else changes. Modifiable factors can be changed. Heart disease adds high blood pressure, high cholesterol and diabetes. Cancer adds sun exposure, some infections, and workplace hazards like asbestos. But look at the overlap: smoking, alcohol, diet, inactivity and body weight raise both. So one prevention effort cuts two of the biggest causes of death at once. And a risk factor raises the chance. It doesn't decide the outcome.

Protective factors lower the chance, or the harm, and they work at three levels. Individual: not smoking, being active, eating well. Health system: screening, which tests people without symptoms, for bowel, breast and cervical cancer, vaccination against the virus behind most cervical cancer. And structural: tobacco control, food labelling, alcohol pricing, walkable suburbs and sun-safe schools. The strongest in our history have been structural. Tobacco control saved more lives than any one decision to quit.

Where and for whom are they changing? Not evenly. Both follow the income gradient, and improvement has been slower for disadvantaged groups, so some gaps widened. Outcomes worsen with remoteness: for heart attacks, it's time to treatment, and for cancer, later diagnosis and travel for care. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples face higher rates and earlier onset of both. Heart disease is under-recognised in women, partly because symptoms can differ. The rule is, improvement reaches the best-resourced groups first.

So, two stories. Cardiovascular disease is, in large part, a prevention story: about half or more of the fall came from fewer people developing it, because policy moves a few big risk factors. Cancer is mostly a detection and treatment story, because it's many diseases. The big exception is lung cancer, where tobacco control worked as it did for the heart. And because cancer gains depend on access, cancer gaps stay stubborn. Yet most spending still goes to treatment, so the case is to shift more toward prevention.
Two things to remember. Deaths down, prevalence up: fewer cases and more survivors, but spending is mostly treatment, so shift toward prevention. And improvement reaches the best-resourced first.

Two exam questions. First. In the year a new screening test is introduced, the recorded incidence of one cancer jumps sharply, but its death rate doesn't change. Explain the most likely reason, and what you'd check over the next few years. Pause here to answer.

Most likely, it's detection, not more disease. The new test finds cancers that already existed, earlier, so recorded new cases jump. If the disease itself were rising, deaths would rise later. So check mortality over the next few years, and the stage at diagnosis, which should shift earlier. The classic mistake is reading a jump in diagnoses as a jump in disease.

Second. A government can fund one of three: more cancer screening, a structural measure on a shared risk factor, or faster heart attack treatment in regional areas. Choose one. Say which measure moves first, who benefits soonest, and whether the gap narrows or widens at first. Pause here to answer.

Say you chose the shared risk factor, like limits on junk food marketing to children. Incidence of both conditions falls, slowly, so mortality moves last, over decades. It reaches everyone without needing them to act, so the gap is less likely to widen. The strongest argument against it: nothing visible for years. The classic mistake is forgetting who benefits first.

So for any condition, read all four measures on the pathway, sort the risk factors, name protective factors at three levels, and ask who's improving. There's room for one more. How do you choose a third condition?
